opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think this is one of the most underappreciated parts of the whole AI safety conversation, because people tend to assume that if the danger comes from software, the solution has to be software too. Better alignment, better refusals, better filters on the model. Those things matter, but I don't think we should bet civilization on them, because we're still very bad at guaranteeing what a large neural network will or won't do. Jailbreaks keep getting found, open-weight models can be fine-tuned to strip out safeguards, and the capabilities keep growing.

So the beautiful thing about biology is that, at the end of the day, to actually hurt anyone you have to make something physical. Knowing how to design a dangerous pathogen isn't the same as having it in a test tube. There's a chokepoint between bits and atoms, and that's where I think we should put a lot more of our defensive effort.

Concretely, that means things like mandatory screening of DNA synthesis orders, so that every commercial synthesizer, and especially benchtop machines, checks sequences against known threats before printing anything. Right now a lot of that screening is voluntary, which is a bit like having airport security that's optional. It means know-your-customer requirements for the companies selling synthesis services and key lab equipment and reagents. It means building the screening into the hardware itself, so a desktop synthesizer simply won't print a dangerous sequence, the same way we'd want tamper-resistant safeguards in other dual-use technology.

And then there's the defensive side in the physical world: better biosurveillance, like wastewater monitoring and metagenomic sequencing so we catch novel outbreaks early, far-UVC lighting that can inactivate airborne pathogens in public spaces, better PPE stockpiles, and the ability to rapidly develop and manufacture countermeasures. These are things that protect us regardless of whether the threat came from an AI, a state program, or nature.

The broader point I'd make is that this is a template. We shouldn't just trust that the AI will be nice; we should design the world so that even if an AI, or a human using one, tries to do something catastrophic, there are hard physical barriers in the way. That's the same philosophy I've argued for with provably safe systems more generally: don't rely on hoping, rely on guarantees. And biology is a domain where we can actually start building those guarantees today, with fairly modest investment, if governments decide to make it a priority rather than leaving it to voluntary industry commitments.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention nucleic acid language models or say they can automate gain-of-function research.

r002.rationale: It calls for mandatory screening of DNA synthesis orders and says sequences should be checked for known threats before printing.

r003.rationale: It notes that AI capabilities keep growing, then argues for stronger physical safeguards, including mandatory synthesis screening, to address AI-enabled catastrophic risks.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think this is actually one of the more hopeful areas, because biology is the one place where the dangerous knowledge has to pass through the physical world before it can hurt anyone. You can't email someone a pandemic. At some point, somebody has to order DNA, acquire reagents, run equipment, and that gives us chokepoints that simply don't exist for, say, cyberattacks.

So the first thing I'd point to is screening at the DNA synthesis level. Right now you can order synthetic DNA from a number of companies, and screening of those orders is still largely voluntary and uneven. That's absurd. If an AI model can walk a motivated person through designing a pathogen, the defense shouldn't be hoping the model refuses. The defense should be that when the sequence shows up at a synthesis company, or increasingly at a benchtop synthesizer, it gets flagged and the order doesn't get filled. We know how to do this. It's a solvable engineering problem, and it's cheap compared to the downside. It should be mandatory, and it should be international, because the DNA will just get ordered from whichever jurisdiction doesn't check.

The second layer is the hardware itself. Benchtop synthesizers and cloud labs are becoming more capable and more widespread, and I'd argue they should have screening built in, the way we expect safety interlocks on industrial machinery. You don't rely on the operator's good intentions. You build the constraint into the device.

The third layer is the one people underrate, which is making the world robust so that even a successful attempt doesn't become a catastrophe. Better pathogen surveillance, wastewater monitoring, far-UVC lighting in public spaces, rapid vaccine platforms, stockpiles of good respirators. These are defenses that work regardless of who the attacker is or what tools they used. And a lot of them are just good public health investments that pay off against natural pandemics too.

Now, I want to be clear about what physical safeguards can't do. They don't address the AI side of the problem at all. If we build systems that are smarter than us and we lose control of them, the fact that a DNA synthesizer has a screening module is not going to save us. So I think of biosecurity hardening as a necessary layer that buys time and closes off the easiest paths for human misuse, but it's not a substitute for actually governing the models themselves, with real safety standards the way we have for every other powerful technology. We'd never accept a nuclear industry where the only safety measure was that the bombs are hard to deliver. We shouldn't accept it for AI either.

But if you ask me what's the lowest-hanging fruit that governments could pick this year, it's mandatory gene synthesis screening. There's no good argument against it, and the longer we wait, the more the models improve while the screening doesn't.

r001.rationale: The response says an AI model could help someone design a pathogen, but does not state that nucleic acid language models can automate gain-of-function research.

r002.rationale: It calls for mandatory screening of DNA synthesis orders so potentially dangerous pathogen sequences are flagged and not filled.

r003.rationale: It says models will improve while screening does not, and argues that the delay makes mandatory screening more urgent.

astra-6.text:
I think physical safeguards are a very important layer of defense, because even if an AI can tell someone how to make a dangerous pathogen, that information still has to be turned into something physical. You need biological material, equipment, and some way of producing it. Those are opportunities to intervene.

For example, you can screen orders for synthetic DNA and verify who’s ordering it. And ideally, you want safeguards built into the equipment itself, so that bypassing a website’s screening doesn’t simply give you an unmonitored route to manufacturing something dangerous. That’s an engineering challenge, and it’s also a coordination challenge: if safeguards exist in only one country, people can go elsewhere.

But I wouldn’t claim that this solves the whole problem. Biology is complicated, and you can’t assume you’ll recognize every dangerous sequence in advance. You want multiple layers of protection, including limits on the AI assistance that makes an attack easier, safeguards around physical production, and better detection and response if something goes wrong. The point is to make sure that a failure in one layer doesn’t automatically become a catastrophe.

r002.rationale: It suggests screening synthetic DNA orders, but does not propose that screening be mandatory.

r003.rationale: It mentions AI-related biological risks, but does not say that advances in AI make nucleic acid synthesis screening policies more urgent.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to recognize that information and physical things are very different. An AI might tell someone how to make a dangerous pathogen, but that pathogen still has to be produced in the physical world. You need equipment, materials, and some way of getting the relevant DNA synthesized. Those are places where we can put safeguards.

For example, you can require screening of DNA synthesis orders, so that someone can’t simply order the ingredients for a dangerous virus without triggering scrutiny. And you want those safeguards to be difficult to bypass, with broad enough adoption that you can’t just go to another supplier.

But I wouldn’t treat that as a complete solution. Biology is complicated, and a sufficiently capable AI might find ways around the barriers we know how to build today. So physical safeguards are an important layer of defense, alongside making sure we don’t build AI systems that will actively help people circumvent them.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI providing pathogen-making instructions, but does not say nucleic acid language models can automate gain-of-function research.

r002.rationale: It proposes screening DNA synthesis orders so orders for ingredients that could create a dangerous virus trigger scrutiny.

r003.rationale: It notes that a sufficiently capable AI might circumvent current barriers, but does not state that advances in AI increase the urgency of screening policies.
